title: Trigonometry
description: From side ratios in right triangles to the unit circle, repeating graphs, identities and the vector and wave problems they solve.
audience: A capable adult who knows right-triangle distances and similar shapes from Discere's geometry course and can rearrange simple formulas.
outcomes: You'll be able to find sides and angles of any triangle.
You'll be able to read exact values for 30, 45 and 60 degrees and work in radians.
You'll be able to read any angle's sine and cosine from the unit circle.
You'll be able to read and fit amplitude, period, shift and midline for a repeating quantity.
You'll be able to solve basic trigonometric equations and use the main identities.
You'll be able to resolve vectors into components and combine waves.

sources.title: OpenStax, Precalculus 2e (Chapters 5 to 10: trigonometric functions, identities, applications)
OpenStax, College Physics 2e (vectors and periodic motion applications)
NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, Chapter 4 Elementary Functions
NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, Solar Calculator and equations
NOAA Tides and Currents, Harmonic constituents

modules.title: Triangles and their ratios
modules.summary: Ratios that survive scaling, solving right triangles, exact values and triangles with no right angle.

modules.title: Circles and waves
modules.summary: Radians, the unit circle and the graphs that repeat.

modules.title: Identities, equations and uses
modules.summary: Relationships that always hold, solving with them, and trig applied to vectors and sums of waves.

lessons.title: Ratios that survive scaling
lessons.objective: Define sine, cosine and tangent as side ratios and use them to find a ratio from a given triangle.

concepts.title: Sine, cosine, tangent
concepts.summary: For an acute angle in a right triangle: sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent.

concepts.title: Why ratios are fixed
concepts.summary: Similar triangles have equal side ratios, so the ratios depend only on the angle.

misconceptions: The ratios depend on the size of the triangle. They depend on the angle only: a 6-8-10 triangle gives the same as 3-4-5.
Opposite and adjacent are fixed labels. They are relative to the angle chosen.
The hypotenuse can be opposite. It is never opposite or adjacent; it is the side across from the right angle.
sequence: Recall similar triangles from the geometry course.
Scale a 3-4-5 triangle and show the ratios do not change.
Name the sides relative to a chosen angle.
Define the three ratios and call them sine, cosine and tangent.
Read the ratio for a given angle off a table or calculator.
examples: 3-4-5 triangle: for the angle opposite 3, sin = 0.6, cos = 0.8, tan = 0.75. The 6-8-10 triangle gives the same.
Legs 5 and 12 give hypotenuse 13: sin of the angle opposite 5 is 5/13 = 0.385.

figures.shows: right_triangle with a = 3, b = 4, then a = 6, b = 8 as a second case.
figures.learnerAction: Switch cases and compare the three ratios.

figures.shows: A right triangle with opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse labels that move when the angle is changed from A to B.

questionPlan.sample: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. What is the sine of the angle opposite the shorter leg, to three decimals?
A right triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. What is the tangent of the angle opposite the side of length 4, as a decimal to three places?
For angle A in a right triangle, which ratio is opposite over adjacent?

historyNotes: The sine function in its modern chord-half form came from Indian astronomers, written in Sanskrit texts of the Gupta period; the Latin word sinus came from a mistranslation of an Arabic word.

lessons.title: Solving right triangles
lessons.objective: Find missing sides with sin, cos and tan and missing angles with their inverses.

concepts.title: Find a side
concepts.summary: Choose the ratio that links the known and wanted sides, then multiply or divide.

concepts.title: Inverse functions
concepts.summary: arcsin, arccos and arctan return the angle from a ratio.

misconceptions: Always use sine. The right ratio depends on which sides are involved.
The angle mode on a calculator does not matter. Degree and radian mode give different results.
arcsin(x) is 1/sin(x). It is the inverse function, not the reciprocal.
sequence: Elevation angle problem: height of a flagpole from distance and angle.
Choose the ratio by listing the sides involved (SOH CAH TOA as a memory aid).
Rearrange to get the unknown.
Find an angle from two sides with an inverse function.
Check the answer is plausible: hypotenuse longest, angle shape.
examples: Stand 20 m from a flagpole; eye height 1.6 m; the angle of elevation to the top is 35 degrees. Height = 20 tan 35 + 1.6 = 14.0 + 1.6 = 15.6 m.
A ramp rises 1.2 m over 10 m of run: angle = arctan(0.12) = 6.84 degrees.

figures.shows: right_triangle with a = 14 and b = 20 as one case, a = 1.2 and b = 10 as another.

questionPlan.sample: A 6 m ladder leans at 70 degrees to the ground. How high up the wall does it reach, in metres to two decimals?
A 12 m cable runs from the top of a 9 m pole to the ground. What angle does it make with the ground, in degrees to one decimal?
In a right triangle you know the opposite side and the adjacent side. Which function gives the angle?

lessons.title: Angles with exact answers
lessons.objective: Derive exact trig values for 30, 45 and 60 degrees from two triangles.

concepts.title: Special triangles
concepts.summary: Half a square gives 45-45-90 with sides 1, 1, sqrt 2. Half an equilateral triangle gives 30-60-90 with sides 1, sqrt 3, 2.

concepts.title: Exact values
concepts.summary: sin 30 = 1/2, sin 45 = sqrt2/2, sin 60 = sqrt3/2; cos is the same read backwards; tan 45 = 1, tan 60 = sqrt 3.

misconceptions: The exact values are memorised from a table. They come directly from two triangles that can be drawn from memory.
sin 60 is twice sin 30. It is sqrt3/2 = 0.866 against 0.5; sine is not proportional to angle.
The values are approximations from a calculator. They are exact surds.
sequence: Split a square along its diagonal: legs 1, hypotenuse sqrt 2 from Pythagoras.
Read sin 45, cos 45 and tan 45.
Split an equilateral triangle of side 2 in half: base 1, height sqrt 3.
Read off sin and cos for 30 and 60 and note the swap.
Use the triangles to solve a problem exactly.
examples: A 45-45-90 triangle with hypotenuse 10 has legs 10/sqrt2 = 7.07.
A 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 10 has legs 5 and 5 sqrt3 = 8.66.

figures.shows: right_triangle with a = 1, b = 1 and then a = 1, b = 1.732 (the second approximates sqrt 3).

questionPlan.sample: A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 10. How long is the longer leg, to two decimals?
What is tan 45 degrees?
What is the exact value of sin 60 degrees?

lessons.title: Triangles with no right angle
lessons.objective: Solve any triangle with the laws of sines and cosines and find its area.

concepts.title: Law of cosines
concepts.summary: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab cos C: Pythagoras with a correction for the angle between a and b.

concepts.title: Law of sines
concepts.summary: a / sin A = b / sin B = c / sin C.

misconceptions: The law of sines solves every triangle. Two sides with the angle between them need the law of cosines.
A triangle's angles with a given sine are unique. An angle and its supplement have the same sine, so side-side-angle can give two triangles.
The area needs a perpendicular height. Area = 1/2 a b sin C needs only two sides and the angle between.
sequence: Split a general triangle into two right triangles with a height.
Derive the law of cosines from that split and check C = 90 recovers Pythagoras.
Law of sines for angle-angle-side.
Pick the law from what is given (SAS, SSS, AAS).
Area from two sides and the included angle.
examples: A = 40 degrees, B = 60 degrees, a = 10: b = 10 sin 60 / sin 40 = 13.47.

figures.shows: Triangle with height dropped, labelled for the law of cosines; switchable cases SAS, SSS and AAS.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the given parts and see which law the diagram highlights.

questionPlan.sample: Two sides are 7 and 10 with an included angle of 60 degrees. What is the third side, in units to two decimals?
Two sides are 7 and 10 with an included angle of 60 degrees. What is the area, to one decimal?
A triangle has sides 5, 6 and 7. What is its largest angle, in degrees to one decimal?

lessons.title: Turning in radians
lessons.objective: Convert between degrees and radians and use arc length and sector area.

concepts.title: Radian
concepts.summary: The angle at the centre of a circle that subtends an arc equal to the radius; 2 pi radians make a full turn.

concepts.title: Arc and sector
concepts.summary: Arc length s = r theta and sector area A = 1/2 r^2 theta, with theta in radians.

misconceptions: Radians are an arbitrary alternative to degrees. They make arc and area formulas free of constants.
pi radians is 3.14 degrees. It is 180 degrees.
Use s = r theta with degrees. Theta must be in radians.
sequence: Wrap a radius around the rim: one radian.
Count how many radius lengths fit around: 2 pi.
Convert both ways with 180 degrees = pi radians.
Arc length and sector area.
Real use: 1 degree of latitude along a meridian is about 111 km.
examples: 150 degrees = 150 x pi/180 = 5 pi/6 = 2.618 rad.
r = 5 m, theta = 1.2 rad: arc = 6 m, sector area = 1/2 x 25 x 1.2 = 15 m2. Earth (R = 6,371 km): 1 degree is 6,371 x pi/180 = 111.2 km.

figures.shows: circle with radius 5, with an arc of one radius marked.
figures.learnerAction: Switch between radius 5 and radius 3 and see the angle stays 1 rad.

figures.shows: Circle with sector angle slider as fixed cases: 1, 2, pi/2 rad.

questionPlan.sample: Convert 150 degrees to radians, to three decimals.
A circle has radius 5 m. A sector has angle 1.2 radians. What is the arc length in metres?
The same sector has radius 5 m and angle 1.2 radians. What is its area in square metres?

lessons.title: The unit circle
lessons.objective: Read sine, cosine and tangent of any angle from a point on the unit circle.

concepts.title: Unit circle
concepts.summary: The point at angle theta on the circle of radius 1 is (cos theta, sin theta).

concepts.title: Reference angle
concepts.summary: The acute angle to the x-axis; the trig values match it up to sign.

misconceptions: Sine and cosine are only defined up to 90 degrees. Moving the point around the circle extends them to all angles.
Signs are memorised. They come from the position of the point: cosine is the x value and sine is the y value.
tan 135 is positive. It is sine over cosine, and sine is positive and cosine negative in the second quadrant, so it is negative.
sequence: Put the right triangle in a circle of radius 1: the legs become the coordinates.
Extend the angle beyond 90 degrees: the point continues, the coordinates change sign.
Reference angles to reuse the special values.
Negative angles and angles over 360.
The identity from the coordinates (preview).
examples: 120 degrees: reference angle 60, point (-0.5, 0.866). 210 degrees: reference 30, sin = -0.5, cos = -0.866.

figures.shows: The unit circle with a draggable point and readouts of x and y.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the point to an angle.

figures.shows: Sine and cosine of the angle against angle, linked to the point.

questionPlan.sample: What is sin 210 degrees?
What is the x coordinate of the point at 120 degrees on the unit circle?
In which quadrant are both sine and cosine negative?

lessons.title: Graphs that repeat
lessons.objective: Read amplitude, period, shift and midline from a sine or cosine formula.

concepts.title: Amplitude and period
concepts.summary: y = A sin(Bx): amplitude A, period 2 pi / B.

concepts.title: Shift and midline
concepts.summary: y = A sin(B(x - C)) + D shifts right by C and moves the midline to D.

misconceptions: The period of sin(2x) is 4 pi. B doubles the speed, so the period halves to pi.
A negative A or shifted C changes the amplitude. Amplitude is the size of A; a minus sign reflects the graph.
The graph is zero at the origin. The midline and shift move it; cosine starts at a maximum.
sequence: Unroll the unit circle: height against angle.
Amplitude (size), period (length), midline (centre) and shift (start).
Change one parameter at a time.
Match formula to graph in both directions.
Tie to wave and spring formulas in physics.
examples: y = 3 sin(2x) + 1: amplitude 3, period pi, midline 1, maximum 4, minimum -2.
y = sin(pi x / 6): period 2 pi/(pi/6) = 12.

figures.shows: y = 3 sin(2x) + 1 with a faded y = sin x for comparison, plus a second case y = 2 cos(x) - 5.

questionPlan.sample: What is the period of y = sin(pi x / 6)?
What is the maximum value of y = 3 sin(2x) + 1?
What is the amplitude of y = 2 cos(x) - 5?

lessons.title: Modelling cycles
lessons.objective: Fit a sine or cosine model to a cycle and use it to predict.

concepts.title: Fit a periodic model
concepts.summary: From the maximum, minimum and period: A = (max - min)/2, D = (max + min)/2, B = 2 pi / period.

concepts.title: Use the model
concepts.summary: Evaluate it at a time, or solve for the time when it reaches a value.

misconceptions: Pick sine or cosine by guessing and adjust until it fits. The start of the cycle tells you which is simpler.
A model fits forever. Real cycles drift and have limits; the model describes the repeating part.
Time to reach a height is found from the graph by eye alone. Solving the equation also gives the second time in each cycle.
sequence: Ferris wheel: centre 12 m, radius 10 m, period 40 s, starting at the bottom.
Read off amplitude, midline and period, then write h(t) = 12 - 10 cos(2 pi t / 40).
Evaluate at a time.
Solve for the time to reach a given height.
Other cycles: daylight length, tides (NOAA constituents), seasonal temperature.

figures.shows: h(t) for the Ferris wheel and a second case of day length against day number.
The wheel with a rider point and a height-time trace beside it.

questionPlan.sample: A wheel has centre 12 m high, radius 10 m, period 40 s and starts at the bottom. Using h = 12 - 10 cos(2 pi t / 40), what is h at t = 20 s, in metres?
With the same wheel, when is the rider first at 17 m? Give the time in seconds to two decimals.
A tide ranges from 0.4 m to 2.4 m. What is the amplitude of a model for it, in metres?

lessons.title: Identities that always hold
lessons.objective: Use the Pythagorean identity, the double-angle formulas and the angle-sum formulas.

concepts.title: Pythagorean identity
concepts.summary: sin^2 theta + cos^2 theta = 1, because (cos, sin) lies on the unit circle.

concepts.title: Angle formulas
concepts.summary: sin(a + b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b; sin 2a = 2 sin a cos a; cos 2a = 1 - 2 sin^2 a.

misconceptions: sin(a + b) = sin a + sin b. Try a = b = 30 degrees: 0.866 against 1.
sin^2 x means sin(x^2). It means (sin x) squared.
An identity is an equation to solve. It is true for every angle; you use it to rewrite.
sequence: Pythagoras on the unit circle gives the first identity.
Use it to find cosine from sine, with the sign from the quadrant.
Angle-sum formula (stated with a geometric picture, then used).
Double angle as a special case.
Find an exact value such as sin 75.
examples: sin theta = 0.6 with theta in quadrant 2: cos = -0.8, sin 2 theta = 2 x 0.6 x (-0.8) = -0.96, cos 2 theta = 1 - 2 x 0.36 = 0.28.

figures.shows: Unit circle point with the right triangle and sin^2 and cos^2 squares displayed.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the point and watch the squares sum to 1.

questionPlan.sample: sin theta = 0.6 and theta is in the second quadrant. What is cos theta?
With sin theta = 0.6 and cos theta = -0.8, what is sin 2 theta?
Use sin(45 + 30) to find sin 75 degrees, to three decimals.

lessons.title: Solving trigonometric equations
lessons.objective: Find all solutions in an interval, including the second angle from the unit circle.

concepts.title: Two solutions per cycle
concepts.summary: sin x = c has solutions at x and pi - x in each cycle; cos x = c has x and 2 pi - x.

concepts.title: Rewrite then solve
concepts.summary: Use identities or factoring to make one function equal to a constant.

misconceptions: The calculator gives all the answers. It returns one angle; the unit circle shows the other.
Dividing both sides by sin x is safe. It loses the solutions where sin x = 0; factor instead.
When the argument is 2x, you only double-check one cycle. Solve for 2x over twice the range.
sequence: Solve sin x = 1/2 on the circle: two points at the same height.
Cosine equations: two points at the same x position.
Equation with multiple angle: solve for 2x over a longer range, then halve.
Factor: 2 sin^2 x = sin x gives sin x = 0 or 1/2.
Check solutions against the interval and by substitution.
examples: sin x = -0.5 on 0 to 360: x = 210 and 330 degrees.
2 sin^2 x = sin x on 0 to 2 pi: sin x = 0 gives 0 and pi; sin x = 1/2 gives pi/6 and 5 pi/6. Four solutions.

figures.shows: y = sin x and the horizontal line y = c with intersections highlighted; cases c = 0.5, c = -0.5.

questionPlan.sample: Solve sin x = -0.5 for 0 to 360 degrees. What is the smaller solution, in degrees?
How many solutions does sin(2x) = 0.5 have for x from 0 to 2 pi?
How many solutions does 2 sin^2 x = sin x have for x from 0 to 2 pi?

lessons.title: Trig for vectors and bearings
lessons.objective: Resolve a vector into components and combine displacements and velocities.

concepts.title: Components
concepts.summary: A vector of size V at angle theta has V cos theta along the axis and V sin theta across it.

concepts.title: Bearing
concepts.summary: A direction measured clockwise from north; east displacement = d sin(bearing), north = d cos(bearing).

misconceptions: Use cos for the horizontal part always. It depends on where the angle is measured from.
Vectors add like numbers. Sizes add only when they point the same way; use components.
A bearing is measured from east like a maths angle. It is measured clockwise from north.
sequence: Break a pulled sled's force into forward and upward parts.
Bearings and compass navigation.
Add two displacements component by component.
Wind and aircraft: ground speed from air speed and wind.
Link to a slope: the weight component along a ramp (physics).
examples: 50 N at 30 degrees above horizontal: horizontal 43.3 N, vertical 25 N.
A ship sails 20 km on bearing 060: east 17.3 km, north 10.0 km. A plane heading east at 200 km/h with a 50 km/h wind from the south has ground speed sqrt(200^2 + 50^2) = 206.2 km/h.

figures.shows: A vector from the origin with component dashed lines; cases for 50 N at 30 degrees and a bearing path.

questionPlan.sample: A 50 N force acts at 30 degrees above horizontal. What is the horizontal component in N, to one decimal?
A ship sails 20 km on bearing 060 degrees. How far east has it moved, in km to one decimal?
A plane flies east at 200 km/h with a 50 km/h wind blowing north. What is its ground speed in km/h to one decimal?

lessons.title: Adding waves
lessons.objective: Combine a cos x + b sin x into one wave and find its amplitude and phase.

concepts.title: Single wave form
concepts.summary: a cos x + b sin x = R cos(x - phi), with R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) and tan phi = b/a.

concepts.title: Same-frequency sums
concepts.summary: Two sinusoids of the same frequency always add to a sinusoid of that frequency.

misconceptions: The amplitudes of two waves add to give the sum's amplitude. They add only when the waves are in phase; otherwise R is smaller.
Different frequencies also give a sinusoid. They do not; they give beats or more complicated shapes.
The phase is arbitrary. It is the angle of the vector (a, b).
sequence: Two waves 3 cos x and 4 sin x: draw them as vectors at right angles.
R is the hypotenuse: 5.
phi is the angle of the vector: arctan(4/3) = 53.13 degrees.
Check the identity with the angle-sum formula.
Link back to physics: adding oscillations and alternating currents.
examples: 3 cos x + 4 sin x = 5 cos(x - 53.13 degrees); its maximum is 5.
6 sin x + 8 cos x = 10 sin(x + 53.13 degrees); the maximum is 10 and occurs where x + 53.13 = 90, at x = 36.87 degrees.

figures.shows: 3 cos x, 4 sin x and their sum, with the sum's amplitude marked.
figures.learnerAction: Switch a and b between fixed cases (3,4), (5,0), (1,1).

figures.shows: The vector (a, b) with R and phi.

questionPlan.sample: What is the maximum value of 6 sin x + 8 cos x?
3 cos x + 4 sin x = R cos(x - phi). What is phi in degrees, to one decimal?
Two waves of amplitude 3 and 4 and the same frequency add. The sum's amplitude is
questionPlan.answer: Between 1 and 7, depending on their phase
choices: Between 1 and 7, depending on their phase

courseCheck: Mixed items: choose the right ratio and solve a triangle, an exact value, a law of sines or cosines problem, a radian conversion, a unit-circle sign, a parameter read from a formula, a modelling question, a solution count, a component calculation and a combined amplitude. At least three should be applied: a ladder, a bearing and a Ferris wheel or tide.
platformNeeds: A unit-circle figure with a draggable point and a linked sine/cosine trace. coordinate_plane can show the circle and point, but the linked graph panel needs a new figure. Fallback: coordinate_plane plus a separate graph_plot of fixed cases.
A trigonometric graph explorer with sliders for amplitude, period, shift and midline. Fallback: graph_plot cases written out.
A calculator-style numeric answer widget with sin, cos, tan, their inverses and degree/radian mode, so the numeric questions are not blocked by hand arithmetic.
A geometry_explorer shape for a general triangle (SAS, SSS) with computed angles. Fallback: svg_figure.
unverified: All sources: the research environment could not reach the internet (proxy denied every host), so every source is marked verified false. URLs are the standard OpenStax, NIST, NOAA and Clark University locations as remembered.
The history note on the Sanskrit origin of sine and the Latin mistranslation of the Arabic word is from memory; check before using.
The day-length model d(t) = 12 + 4 sin(2 pi (t - 80)/365) is an illustrative approximation for a mid-latitude site, not a NOAA formula.
The tide range example (0.4 m to 2.4 m) is invented for the exercise.
Geometry_explorer's right_triangle takes legs a and b with a minimum of 0.5; the 1.2 and 10 and 1.732 cases fit but the angle readouts have not been confirmed against the component.
